candidates.teaser: A honeybee colony makes decisions more democratically than most human governments — and the method is fascinating.
candidates.video_title: Bees Vote. And They're Better at It Than Us.
candidates.video_description: Honeybee swarms choose a new home through a voting process that rivals human democracy. Scout bees argue, persuade, and eventually reach consensus before the whole colony moves. Nature's parliament is more efficient than ours.
candidates.script: Did you know that a swarm of fifty thousand bees makes decisions more fairly than most human governments? When a colony needs a new home, scout bees fan out and search independently. Each scout returns and performs a waggle dance to campaign for her chosen location. The longer and more enthusiastic the dance, the better the site. Other bees inspect the spots themselves, and only dance for locations they personally approve. No bee can force a vote. The swarm moves only when enough scouts agree. Scientists call this a quorum. So next time democracy feels broken, just remember — bees figured it out four million years ago. Which species do you think is actually smarter?

candidates.topic: The Library of Alexandria wasn't destroyed in one fire
candidates.teaser: Everything you learned about the Library of Alexandria's destruction is probably wrong.
candidates.video_title: The Library of Alexandria Wasn't Burned Down
candidates.video_description: The famous burning of the Library of Alexandria is one of history's most repeated myths. The truth about how ancient knowledge was actually lost is far more complicated — and unsettling. History class left out the real story.
candidates.script: Everyone thinks Julius Caesar accidentally burned down the Library of Alexandria and destroyed all ancient knowledge overnight. That never happened. The Library actually declined slowly over centuries, starved of funding, stripped of scrolls by rival rulers, and gradually abandoned as scholars stopped coming. There was no single catastrophic fire that erased history. The knowledge wasn't lost in one dramatic moment — it simply wasn't copied fast enough, wasn't valued enough, and faded away piece by piece over hundreds of years. Historians say that's actually the more terrifying version of the story. So here's the question — what knowledge are we quietly losing right now, without even noticing?

candidates.teaser: Some humans have trained themselves to see in complete darkness using only sound — just like bats.
candidates.video_title: Some Humans Can Actually See With Sound
candidates.video_description: Human echolocation is a real, trainable skill. Certain blind individuals — and even sighted people — can learn to detect objects using subtle clicking sounds and their own ears. The brain rewires itself to make it possible.
candidates.script: Bats use echolocation to fly in total darkness — but here's what nobody tells you: humans can learn to do the exact same thing. Researchers have documented blind individuals who click their tongues and listen to the returning sound bouncing off walls, trees, and cars to navigate perfectly. Brain scans revealed something extraordinary — their visual cortex, the part meant for seeing, was processing these sound echoes as if they were images. The brain literally rewired itself to see with sound. And it's not just blind people — sighted volunteers learned basic echolocation within weeks of training. So how many other hidden abilities is your brain hiding from you right now?

candidates.teaser: One planet in our solar system is so bizarrely light that it would float in your bathtub — if you had one big enough.
candidates.video_title: Saturn Is So Light It Would Float on Water
candidates.video_description: Saturn is the least dense planet in our solar system — less dense than water itself. If you could place it in an ocean large enough to hold it, it would float. This single fact changes how most people picture gas giants.
candidates.script: Saturn is the second largest planet in the entire solar system — and it would float in water. Not sink. Float. Saturn is made mostly of hydrogen and helium, making it less dense than water itself. Its average density is only 0.69 grams per cubic centimeter, while water is 1. Drop it in an impossibly giant ocean and it bobs right to the surface. Meanwhile, Earth would sink instantly because we're packed with rock and iron. Saturn looks enormous and intimidating with those iconic rings stretching hundreds of thousands of kilometers — but it's essentially a colossal cosmic balloon. That raises a strange question though — if you could stand on Saturn, what exactly would you be standing on?

candidates.topic: Refrigerators nearly destroyed the ozone layer and then we fixed it
candidates.teaser: Refrigerators once tore a hole in the sky the size of a continent — and humans actually managed to fix it.
candidates.video_title: We Accidentally Tore the Sky. Then Fixed It.
candidates.video_description: The ozone hole caused by CFCs in refrigerators and aerosols was one of the worst environmental disasters in human history. The Montreal Protocol of 1987 became the only UN treaty ever signed by every nation on Earth — and it worked. The ozone layer is healing.
candidates.script: In the 1980s, scientists discovered a hole in Earth's ozone layer the size of Antarctica — and the culprit was hiding in every refrigerator and hairspray can on the planet. Chemicals called CFCs were silently eating the atmospheric shield protecting all life from deadly ultraviolet radiation. Skin cancer rates were projected to skyrocket. Then something remarkable happened — every single country on Earth agreed on a solution and signed the Montreal Protocol in 1987, banning the chemicals. It's the only UN treaty ever ratified by every nation. And it actually worked. The ozone layer is measurably healing today. We genuinely fixed a planetary crisis. So why does almost nobody talk about this as humanity's greatest environmental win?
